comparisons.title: Scalability vs elasticity
comparisons.question: Does the workload need to support more load, or adjust capacity automatically with demand?

options.name: Scalability
options.useWhen: Handling more load by adding resources (more or bigger ones).
options.avoidWhen: The scenario asks for automatic adjustment to variable demand.

options.name: Elasticity
options.useWhen: Capacity must grow and shrink automatically with real demand.
options.avoidWhen: The scenario only mentions supporting growth, no automatic adjustment.

differences.b: Pay only for what is used

comparisons.examClue: "Automatically according to demand" = elasticity; just "more users/load" = scalability.

comparisons.title: High availability vs fault tolerance
comparisons.question: Must the system stay operational through partial failures, or keep working correctly despite active failures?

options.name: High availability
options.useWhen: Minimizing downtime (e.g., multiple AZs).
options.avoidWhen: Zero functional impact is required even during the failure.

options.name: Fault tolerance
options.useWhen: The system must keep working correctly with components down.
options.avoidWhen: Reduced downtime is sufficient.

comparisons.examClue: "Keeps working even if X fails" = fault tolerance; "recovers quickly" = high availability.

comparisons.title: Region vs Availability Zone vs edge location
comparisons.question: Which infrastructure level answers the requirement?

options.name: Region
options.useWhen: Choosing where resources live (geography, data residency).
options.avoidWhen: The issue is a single data center failure or static content latency.

options.name: Availability Zone
options.useWhen: Isolating the application from a data center failure (high availability).
options.avoidWhen: The requirement is surviving a full Region failure.

options.name: Edge location
options.useWhen: Caching content close to end users (CloudFront).
options.avoidWhen: You need to run applications: edges do not host workloads.

comparisons.examClue: "Cache near the user" = edge; "survive a data center failure" = multi-AZ; "data in one country" = Region.

comparisons.title: EC2 vs Lambda vs containers (ECS/EKS + Fargate)
comparisons.question: Virtual machine, event-driven functions, or containers for your workload?

options.name: Amazon EC2 (VM)
options.useWhen: Full OS control, continuous and customized workloads.
options.avoidWhen: Brief event-driven tasks, or the team does not want to operate servers.

options.name: AWS Lambda (serverless)
options.useWhen: Brief, intermittent functions triggered by events, with zero administration.
options.avoidWhen: Very long processes or high continuous usage.

options.name: Containers (ECS/EKS/Fargate)
options.useWhen: Package the app with its dependencies and orchestrate multiple instances; Fargate avoids server management.
options.avoidWhen: A simple event function (Lambda is simpler) or full OS control (EC2).

differences.a: EC2: high · Containers: medium · Fargate/Lambda: minimal

comparisons.examClue: "No servers" + brief events = Lambda; "Kubernetes" = EKS; OS control = EC2.

comparisons.title: Amazon ECS vs Amazon EKS
comparisons.question: AWS's own orchestration or managed Kubernetes?

options.name: Amazon ECS
options.useWhen: You want simple container orchestration deeply integrated with AWS.
options.avoidWhen: The team already uses Kubernetes tools and manifests.

options.name: Amazon EKS
options.useWhen: Migrating existing Kubernetes workloads or needing standard portability.
options.avoidWhen: There is no prior Kubernetes experience or requirement.

differences.a: Lower if you are already on AWS
differences.b: Higher if you don't know K8s

comparisons.examClue: When the question mentions Kubernetes, the answer is almost always EKS.

comparisons.title: S3 vs EBS vs EFS
comparisons.question: Objects with URLs, one instance's disk, or a shared file system?

options.name: Amazon S3 (object)
options.useWhen: Static files, backups, data lakes, access by URL/API.
options.avoidWhen: You need to mount a disk or a POSIX file system.

options.name: Amazon EBS (block)
options.useWhen: Persistent disk for ONE instance (OS, databases, boot).
options.avoidWhen: Several instances must share the same files at once.

options.name: Amazon EFS (file)
options.useWhen: Shared file system across MANY Linux instances (POSIX, elastic).
options.avoidWhen: One disk per instance (EBS) or object storage (S3).

comparisons.examClue: "Many instances share folders" = EFS; "one instance's disk" = EBS; "files with URLs" = S3.

comparisons.title: RDS/Aurora vs DynamoDB
comparisons.question: Relational SQL or key-value NoSQL at scale?

options.name: Amazon RDS / Aurora
options.useWhen: Relational schema, joins, SQL transactions, MySQL/PostgreSQL compatibility.
options.avoidWhen: Flexible schema with massive traffic and millisecond latency at any scale.

options.name: Amazon DynamoDB
options.useWhen: NoSQL key-value, flexible schema, massive scale without servers.
options.avoidWhen: You need joins and traditional SQL queries.

comparisons.examClue: "Profiles, sessions, flexible catalog, millions of requests" = DynamoDB; "SQL/relational queries" = RDS.

comparisons.title: Security groups vs network ACLs
comparisons.question: Stateful filter at the instance level or stateless at the subnet level?

options.name: Security group
options.useWhen: Controlling traffic at the instance level; default and stateful (responses flow automatically).
options.avoidWhen: You need explicit inbound and outbound rules at the subnet level.

options.name: Network ACL
options.useWhen: Subnet-level filter, stateless, with numbered rules evaluated in order.
options.avoidWhen: The default per-instance firewall is enough.

comparisons.examClue: "Subnet level" or "stateless" = NACL; "instance level" or "stateful" = security group.

comparisons.title: CloudWatch vs CloudTrail vs Config
comparisons.question: Performance metrics, API auditing, or configuration history?

options.name: Amazon CloudWatch
options.useWhen: Monitoring performance and health: metrics, application logs, alarms.
options.avoidWhen: The question is "who did what and when?" or "how was it configured?".

options.name: AWS CloudTrail
options.useWhen: Auditing actions and API calls: who, what, when, from where.
options.avoidWhen: You need live system performance metrics.

options.name: AWS Config
options.useWhen: Tracking resource configurations and their history, evaluating compliance rules.
options.avoidWhen: You need live metrics or user action logs.

differences.b: Who did what? / How is it configured and did it change?

comparisons.examClue: Performance = CloudWatch; "who created/deleted" = CloudTrail; "configuration changed" = Config.

comparisons.title: SNS vs SQS vs EventBridge
comparisons.question: Notify many, queue work, or route events with rules?

options.name: Amazon SNS
options.useWhen: Publish one message to MANY subscribers at once (push): email, SMS, Lambda.
options.avoidWhen: One consumer must process messages one by one from a queue.

options.name: Amazon SQS
options.useWhen: Queue: producers enqueue and consumers pull (polling); decouple and absorb spikes.
options.avoidWhen: Simultaneous push delivery to several subscribers is required.

options.name: Amazon EventBridge
options.useWhen: Event bus with rule-based routing and advanced filtering across services.
options.avoidWhen: Only a simple queue or a direct notification is needed.

comparisons.examClue: "Notify many" = SNS; "polled queue" = SQS; "route events by rules" = EventBridge.

comparisons.title: AWS Shield vs AWS WAF
comparisons.question: Volumetric network attack (DDoS) or web application exploits (HTTP)?

options.name: AWS Shield
options.useWhen: Protecting against DDoS: network/resource saturation. Standard included free.
options.avoidWhen: The attack is at the application layer: SQLi, XSS, malicious HTTP requests.

options.name: AWS WAF
options.useWhen: Filtering HTTP requests with rules (SQL injection, XSS, geo-blocking).
options.avoidWhen: The problem is a volumetric network flood.

differences.a: Yes: Shield mitigates the flood, WAF filters requests

comparisons.examClue: DDoS → Shield; SQLi/XSS → WAF. They often appear together as distractors.

comparisons.title: GuardDuty vs Inspector vs Macie
comparisons.question: Active threats, software vulnerabilities, or sensitive data in S3?

options.name: Amazon GuardDuty
options.useWhen: Detecting anomalous behavior and active threats (suspicious access, unusual API usage).
options.avoidWhen: You are looking for software vulnerabilities or sensitive data.

options.name: Amazon Inspector
options.useWhen: Scanning for unpatched software vulnerabilities and network exposures.
options.avoidWhen: The concern is ongoing threats or sensitive data.

options.name: Amazon Macie
options.useWhen: Discovering and alerting on personal/sensitive data stored in S3.
options.avoidWhen: You need intrusion detection or vulnerability scanning.

comparisons.examClue: Active threat = GuardDuty; vulnerability = Inspector; personal data in S3 = Macie.

comparisons.title: Budgets vs Cost Explorer vs Pricing Calculator
comparisons.question: Alert, analyze real spend, or estimate before deploying?

options.name: AWS Budgets
options.useWhen: Defining budgets and receiving alerts when a threshold is exceeded (or forecasted to be).
options.avoidWhen: You want to analyze trends of already incurred spend.

options.name: AWS Cost Explorer
options.useWhen: Visualizing, grouping, and forecasting real spend (past and present).
options.avoidWhen: The architecture does not exist yet and a quote is needed.

options.name: AWS Pricing Calculator
options.useWhen: Estimating the cost of an architecture BEFORE implementing it.
options.avoidWhen: You need budget alerts or real spend analysis.

comparisons.examClue: "Before implementing" = Pricing Calculator; "threshold alert" = Budgets; "where the money goes" = Cost Explorer.

comparisons.title: On-Demand vs Reserved/Savings Plans vs Spot vs Dedicated Hosts
comparisons.question: Which purchasing option, based on stability and interruptibility of the workload?

options.name: On-Demand
options.useWhen: New, variable, or short-term workloads with no commitment.
options.avoidWhen: Stable, predictable long-term usage (you pay more).

options.name: Reserved / Savings Plans
options.useWhen: Constant, predictable usage with a 1-3 year commitment.
options.avoidWhen: The workload is intermittent or interruptible.

options.name: Spot
options.useWhen: Flexible, interruptible jobs (batch, testing) with the largest discount.
options.avoidWhen: Critical workloads that cannot tolerate interruptions.

options.name: Dedicated Hosts
options.useWhen: Per-socket/core licensing requirements or physical compliance.
options.avoidWhen: You only seek savings or logical isolation control.

comparisons.examClue: Interruptible + max savings = Spot; stable 24/7 = Reserved/Savings; physical licensing = Dedicated Host.

comparisons.title: Rehost vs Replatform vs Refactor
comparisons.question: How much does the application change during migration?

options.name: Rehost (lift and shift)
options.useWhen: Migrate fast with no changes: replicate servers as they are.
options.avoidWhen: There is time or a mandate to modernize the platform.

options.name: Replatform (lift, tinker and shift)
options.useWhen: Small, low-risk changes: e.g., moving the DB to Aurora with DMS.
options.avoidWhen: Zero changes are required or a full redesign is sought.

options.name: Refactor / Re-architect
options.useWhen: Redesigning to maximize cloud benefits (microservices, serverless).
options.avoidWhen: Priority is migration speed and low risk.

comparisons.examClue: "No changes" = Rehost; "the DB engine changes" = Replatform; "microservices/redesign" = Refactor.

comparisons.title: AWS Support plans
comparisons.question: Which plan for the criticality and size of the environment?

options.name: Basic support
options.useWhen: Documentation, whitepapers, forums, and re:Post. Included free.
options.avoidWhen: You need technical support from AWS people.

options.name: Developer Support
options.useWhen: Test/development environments: email help during business hours.
options.avoidWhen: Production workloads requiring 24/7 support.

options.name: Business Support
options.useWhen: Production: 24/7 phone/chat support with fast response times.
options.avoidWhen: Massive critical workloads that need a TAM.

options.name: Enterprise / On-Ramp
options.useWhen: Large critical workloads: TAM, minute-level responses, concierge.
options.avoidWhen: Small budgets or non-critical workloads.
